content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.
14	
15	A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colors which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object.
16	
17	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.

Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.

Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].

Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.

A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.

A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colors which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object.

A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.

A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.

There remains a need for a cordless handheld vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

findings.title: Background says US-5374090-A indicates power-source state "rather than the state of the grip", which that reference's own claims contradict
findings.where: draft/05-background.md, line 15 (paragraph beginning "A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers"), final sentence; the same characterisation is reused at line 23 ("a condition unrelated to grip (battery state)")
findings.detail: The draft's factual recital of US-5374090-A is accurate (the abstract does say the LEDs "indicate to an operator whether or not the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object", and claim 2 does determine sufficiency from voltage drops across resistors). But the concluding sentence asserts a flat negative that the same file denies: prior_art/US-5374090-A.md, claim 1, recites "means for indicating to an operator whether said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object", with a first LED that "illuminates when said means for creating a suction force is activated and said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object" and a second LED for insufficient strength. The reference therefore expressly frames the indication as an indication about the grip on the object. What the file supports is the narrower point that the sufficiency is determined electrically, from the voltage drop across the power source, and not from any measurement of the vacuum. As written the sentence characterises the reference in a way its own claim text refuses.
findings.evidence: Draft (05-background.md, line 15): "...light-emitting diodes of different colors which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object."  Source (prior_art/US-5374090-A.md, Claims): "means for indicating to an operator whether said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object, said indicating means comprising: a first light-emitting diode which illuminates when said means for creating a suction force is activated and said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object..."
findings.fix: In draft/05-background.md line 15, replace the final sentence with a statement the file supports: "The sufficiency indicated in that device is determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source rather than from a measurement of the vacuum holding the object." In line 23, replace "on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state)" with "on a determination made from the state of the power source". Change nothing else.

findings.title: Background's blanket "the user is told nothing until the panel is gone" contradicts the draft's own recital of US-10625955-B2
findings.where: draft/05-background.md, line 23 (paragraph beginning "Three shortcomings persist"), first shortcoming
findings.detail: The "First" shortcoming asserts, of "the known powered devices" as a class, that when the leak beats the pump the user is told nothing at all until the load is lost. Eight lines earlier the same Background correctly reports that in US-10625955-B2 warning information relating to pressure is transmitted when the sealed-space pressure falls below the low predetermined pressure, and prior_art/US-10625955-B2.md, claim 10, confirms it. The absolute "told nothing" therefore both overstates what the cited files say and contradicts the draft's own earlier sentence. The supportable point is the one the draft already makes elsewhere: the condition on which those devices signal is fixed with reference to the working vacuum and is not related by the reference to the vacuum still needed to hold the load. I am confident of the contradiction; the fix is a narrowing of the assertion, not a removal of the argument.
findings.evidence: Draft (05-background.md, line 23): "...the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone."  Draft (05-background.md, line 9): "...and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device."  Source (prior_art/US-10625955-B2.md, claim 10): "when the control unit determines that the pressure of the sealed space is smaller than the low predetermined pressure based on the instant pressure information, the control unit transmits warning information to the external electronic device"
findings.fix: In draft/05-background.md line 23, replace "and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone" with "and the person carrying the panel is given no signal that is tied to the vacuum still needed to hold it". Change nothing else in the paragraph.

findings.title: US-5310232-A is twice described as a "suspended" plate assembly, and as equipment "not carried in the hand"; its file states no mounting
findings.where: draft/05-background.md, line 5 ("That equipment is a suspended plate assembly...") and line 25 (paragraph beginning "Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response...")
findings.detail: prior_art/US-5310232-A.md describes a vacuum lifter with a suction plate assembly, projecting annular seals, a vacuum vessel with top and bottom plates, a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source, a pressure pickup and a malfunction alarm, and a remotely operable switch. Nothing in the file says the assembly is suspended, crane-mounted, or that it is not carried in the hand. The draft attributes that mounting to the reference twice, and the entire "Third" shortcoming is built on the attribution. (I attempted to consult the underlying publication with tools/patent_lookup.py; the corpus is unavailable, so the prior_art/ file is the only authority.) The contrast the draft actually needs is available from the files without any mounting assertion: US-5310232-A supplies a second, emergency vacuum source started by a switch, and US-10518985-B2 supplies a controller that limits or alters machine functions — remedies that a cordless handheld lifter, by the inventor's own framing, does not have.
findings.evidence: Draft (05-background.md, line 5): "That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source..."  Draft (05-background.md, line 25): "Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A]..."  Source (prior_art/US-5310232-A.md, Abstract/Claims): "a vacuum lifter to transport loads with an adhesion surface and comprises at least one suction head with at least one projecting annular seal on its suction side" / "a) a suction plate assembly; b) at least first and second seals projecting from sid assembly and defining therebetween a vacuum chamber" — no statement of how the assembly is supported.
findings.fix: In draft/05-background.md line 5, replace "That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with" with "That equipment is a plate assembly with". In line 25, replace the first sentence and the following clause with: "Third, the remedies that the known equipment applies to a failing grip are remedies a cordless handheld lifter does not have. A plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]." Leave the remainder of the paragraph ("A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it...") unchanged.
